content: The study included patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who were carriers of the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). Among these, three patients were co-infected with HIV and were treatment-naïve. Quantitative testing was performed using the Determine CMIA assay, Architect 203, and Espline 773. Samples were collected from the general community and tested using various methods, including whole blood (capillary and venous), serum, and plasma. The diagnostic accuracy of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) was compared to enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) and nucleic acid tests (NATs) as reference standards. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed. Fifteen studies were judged to have a high risk of bias, with ten of these being case-control studies. Other studies with high bias risk included those involving blood donors and highly selected populations, such as patients with known hepatitis B. Eight studies were deemed to have high applicability concerns, particularly those published over ten years ago or using tests no longer commercially available. Seven studies were identified as having a high risk of bias in the index test domain, primarily due to a lack of blinding during the interpretation of test results. Similarly, five studies were judged to have a high risk of bias in the reference standard domain, with 17 studies being unclear due to insufficient reporting of blinding or utilization of the reference tests. Bias related to flow and timing was predominantly due to a lack of reported time differences between the index and reference assays, although most studies were considered low risk as they used the same sample for both tests. The pooled diagnostic accuracy of RDTs compared to EIAs was evaluated across 21 studies, involving 63 data points and 25 RDT brands. These studies used 15 EIA reference assays and included a total of 36,919 samples, with sample sizes ranging from 25 to 3,983 (mean 586). The studies were conducted in various countries, including China, Ghana, Cambodia, and Vietnam. Significant heterogeneity was observed between studies. For RDTs compared to NATs, three articles contributed nine data points evaluating seven RDTs using 1,710 serum or plasma samples. Sample sizes ranged from 74 to 950 (mean 190). Notably, 1,440 samples were derived from the same 240 patients in one case-control study evaluating six tests. Only one study used plasma samples. The clinical performance of RDTs in HIV-positive and HIV-negative individuals was also assessed. Five articles contributed six data points evaluating three RDTs against an EIA reference, using a total of 3,434 samples from 2,566 patients. Sample sizes ranged from 75 to 838. For HIV-negative individuals, one article contributed four data points evaluating three RDTs using 1,624 samples from 997 patients, with sample sizes ranging from 175 to 773. The performance of RDTs was further stratified by specimen type, study design, and publication date. Seven studies evaluated RDTs using whole blood (capillary or venous), contributing 11 data points and involving 13,731 samples. Ten articles using a case-control design contributed 21 data points evaluating 13 RDTs with a total of 7,258 samples. Additionally, seven articles evaluated RDTs in blood donors, contributing 19 data points and involving 6,881 samples. Stratification by publication date revealed that 21 articles published before and after 2005 contributed 44 data points evaluating 26 RDTs using 25,261 samples. Nine articles published before 2005 contributed 19 data points evaluating 10 RDTs using 25,253 samples. The performance of specific RDT brands was also analyzed. Determine HBsAg was the most frequently evaluated brand, with ten articles contributing 12 data points using 7,553 samples. Binax NOW HBsAg was evaluated in three articles published before 2007, contributing six data points using 3,550 samples. VIKIA HBsAg was evaluated in three articles published after 2010, contributing three data points using 5,242 samples. Serodia HBsAg was evaluated in three articles published before 2000, contributing three data points using 1,040 samples. The pooled accuracy of RDTs evaluated against a CMIA reference was assessed in five articles, contributing nine data points and involving 4,513 samples. Sample sizes ranged from 178 to 838 (mean 501). The studies demonstrated varying levels of sensitivity and specificity, with significant heterogeneity observed across studies. The GRADE assessment for the use of RDTs in diagnosing HBsAg in HIV-negative individuals indicated very low quality of evidence for true positives and low quality for true negatives. For HIV-positive individuals, the evidence quality was very low for true positives and moderate for true negatives. Factors contributing to downgrades included risk of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency across studies.
